problems.stem: A reflection on a unit taught with an AI tool reads: "The lesson went really well and students were engaged." Which revision makes it an evidence-based reflection rather than an impression?
options: "The lesson went really well and students seemed very engaged and happy."
"Exit-ticket scores rose from 58% to 81%, but the 4 students using the printed fallback averaged 12 points lower, so the tool may have widened a gap I will check next week."
"I felt confident and the energy in the room was high."
"Most students said they liked the tool when I asked."
problems.explanation: Evidence-based reflection cites specific observed data, including disconfirming evidence, not feelings or general engagement claims.

problems.stem: A reviewer annotates a reflection: "You only describe the evidence that supports keeping the tool. What did you see that argued against it?" What practice does this note ask for?
options: Add more praise for the tool to balance the tone.
Seek and report disconfirming evidence, so the reflection weighs both supporting and counter-evidence before concluding.
Remove the analysis and keep only the conclusion.
Cite a published study that agrees with the conclusion.
problems.explanation: Sound reflection actively looks for evidence against its own conclusion, not just evidence that confirms it.

problems.stem: A teacher asks BigAL to write a reflection on her own AI-tool lesson. Why does this most undermine the reflection even if the prose is excellent?
options: A reflection's purpose is to surface the teacher's own observed evidence and reasoning; a model cannot have observed her classroom, so it can only invent plausible claims.
The reflection would be longer than required.
AI reflections are always shorter than human ones.
problems.explanation: Reflection depends on the practitioner's own situated evidence; an AI-authored reflection has no observed data to ground it.

problems.stem: A reflection concludes the AI tool worked because the class average rose 10 points the same week the tool launched. Which reasoning move would make the conclusion more defensible?
options: Round the gain up to a more impressive number.
Consider rival explanations (a review day, an easier quiz, test practice) before attributing the gain to the tool.
Drop the data and rely on how the lesson felt.
Conclude the tool worked because the gain is large.
problems.explanation: Evidence-based reflection checks rival explanations before attributing an outcome to one cause; correlation in one week is weak evidence.
